plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional cutaway of a cylindrical capacitor drawn in perspective, extending from the near end at the lower left toward the far end at the upper right. Two concentric conducting cylinders share a common axis: a narrow inner cylinder whose visible near face is crowded with plus signs, and a much wider outer shell whose surface carries minus signs spaced along its length and around its near rim. In the near end view, short red arrows labeled 'E' radiate outward from the inner cylinder across the annular gap to the inner wall of the outer shell, filling the gap uniformly in every radial direction. An orange dashed cylinder of intermediate radius is drawn between the two conductors, appearing as dashed ellipses at both ends joined by dashed lines running the length of the device; a curved leader from the top labels it 'Gaussian surface'. At the far end three arrows fan out from a point on the axis, labeled 'R1', 'r', and 'R2' in order of increasing length. Nesting the dashed surface between the two conductor radii shows precisely which charge it encloses. The geometry sets up the flux calculation that gives the capacitance of a coaxial pair carrying charges plus Q and minus Q.

elements: inner conducting cylinder (small radius R1) shown with positive charge '+' signs on its surface and near end cap
outer conducting shell (radius R2) shown semi-transparent cutaway with negative charge '−' signs spaced along its surface and near rim
annular gap between the two conductors (empty dielectric region)
orange dashed cylindrical Gaussian surface of intermediate radius r — dashed ellipses at both ends joined by two dashed longitudinal lines
'Gaussian surface' label with a curved leader arrow pointing to the dashed surface
red radial E-field arrows in the near end face, pointing outward from the inner cylinder across the gap to the outer shell, labeled 'E'
fan of three black arrows at the far end face from a point on the axis, labeled 'R1', 'r', 'R2' in order of increasing length
common cylinder axis running the length of the device

interactions.label: Gaussian radius r
interactions.teaches: Moving the dashed Gaussian surface from R1 toward R2 keeps the enclosed charge fixed at +Q (only the inner conductor is enclosed), while the E arrows at the surface shrink as 1/r — the field in the gap falls off with distance from the axis

interactions.label: Region
interactions.teaches: E exists only in the annular gap: inside the inner conductor and outside the outer shell the enclosed net charge and field vanish — selecting each zone highlights it and shows where the Gaussian surface encloses charge
Rotating the cutaway reveals the 3D concentric structure — that the dashed surface is a full coaxial cylinder, not just a circle in the end face

demo_steps.title: Surface midway in the gap
demo_steps.narration: With r midway between R1 and R2, the dashed cylinder encloses only the inner conductor's +Q. Red E arrows pierce the surface radially, uniform all around.

demo_steps.title: Push r toward R2
demo_steps.narration: Slide r out toward R2. The enclosed charge is unchanged, but the E arrows at the surface shorten — E = λ/(2πε₀r) decreases as 1/r while flux stays constant.

demo_steps.title: Inside the conductor
demo_steps.narration: Switch to r < R1: the region inside the inner conductor highlights, no charge is enclosed, and the E arrows vanish — the field inside a conductor is zero.

demo_steps.title: Outside both cylinders
demo_steps.narration: Switch to r > R2: the exterior highlights. The surface now encloses +Q and −Q, net zero, so again E = 0 — field lives only in the gap.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Coaxial cylinders aligned along the world X axis (screen: running from near end lower-left to far end upper-right), length ~8 units. Inner conductor: radius R1 = 1.0 world units, solid light-steel-blue. Outer shell: inner radius R2 = 2.0, thin wall (~0.15), rendered semi-transparent blue-grey (#aab4d4, opacity ~0.3) so the interior is visible. Gaussian surface: orange (#e8912d) dashed cylinder of radius r (default 1.5), drawn as dashed rings at both end faces plus two dashed longitudinal lines top and bottom. Charge signs: '+' glyphs (dark) clustered on the inner cylinder's near end cap and scattered on its wall; '−' glyphs spaced along the outer shell's length and around its near rim. E-field arrows: red (#cc2222), ~8 arrows radiating in the near end face plane from r = R1 to r = R2, arrow length ∝ 1/r. Far-end face: three black arrows fanning from the axis point, lengths R1, r, R2, labeled 'R1', 'r', 'R2'. E = λ/(2πε₀r) for R1 < r < R2, zero elsewhere; Q_enclosed = +Q only when r > R1 and r < R2.
interactionPlan.notes: Use dashed-line materials (THREE.LineDashedMaterial with computed line distances) for the Gaussian surface rings and rails. Update Gaussian cylinder radius and E-arrow lengths reactively on slider change; fade arrows to zero opacity with a quick shrink when the region toggle places r outside the gap. Highlight the active region with a soft translucent colored band; keep '+'/'−' glyphs as sprites so they stay legible. Camera: low elevation, axis receding to the right to match the source.

authoredContext:
A cylindrical capacitor consists of two concentric, conducting cylinders (the figure). The inner cylinder, of radius R1, may either be a shell or be completely solid. The outer cylinder is a shell of inner radius R2. We assume that the length of each cylinder is l and that the excess charges +Q and −Q reside on the inner and outer cylinders, respectively.

With edge effects ignored, the electrical field between the conductors is directed radially outward from the common axis of the cylinders. Using the Gaussian surface shown in the figure, we have

A cylindrical capacitor consists of two concentric, conducting cylinders. Here, the charge on the outer surface of the inner cylinder is positive (indicated by +) and the charge on the inner surface of the outer cylinder is negative (indicated by −).

Figure shows two concentric cylinders. The inner one, with radius R1 has positive signs on it. The outer one, with radius R2 has negative signs on it. Arrows marked E are shown radiating from the inner one to the outer one. A third cylinder, with radius r, is shown as a dotted line between the two. This is labeled Gaussian surface.

discrepancies: Colored region-highlight bands (blue/green/purple translucent cylinders) tint the conductors and change the bluish color scheme of the source
Extra annotation labels '+Q (inner conductor)' and '−Q (outer shell)' that the source does not have

Source shows E arrows on the left end face and the R1/r/R2 fan on the right end face; generated figure crams both end-face details and the extra labels together, making the end regions busier than the source

The source shows the Gaussian surface as a thin dashed cylinder between the two conductors; the generated one additionally overlays a solid colored band for the selected region, muddling which element is the Gaussian surface
evaluation.notes: Strong physics content and rich, functional interactions (radius slider, region buttons, demo steps), but the tinted region-highlight bands and extra charge labels deviate from the source's clean composition and bluish color scheme.
action_items: Remove or drastically soften the colored region-highlight bands so the cylinders keep the source's bluish tones and the dashed orange Gaussian surface stays the sole highlight
Drop the extra '+Q (inner conductor)' / '−Q (outer shell)' labels to match the source annotation set (E, Gaussian surface, R1, r, R2)
Clean up rebuildFanLabels to use a proper label-removal API rather than mutating internal _labels, ensuring labels remain robust during interaction
